To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

i) we developed an approach that integrates chromatin modification signatures to improve the specificity of enhancer prediction; ii) we developed an integrative method for enhancer localization that exploits the cross-regulation information between promoter-enhancer regions; and iii) we developed a novel method for the identification of tissue-specific enhancers that integrates expression data, sequence conservation and chromatin modification signatures.

(i) we can identify distal regulatory regions by integrating ChIP-seq data with promoter information, (ii) the use of 4C-seq data in the enhancer search pipeline can improve predictions, and (iii) our framework can be used to predict the expression of genes that are not currently expressed in the cell type of interest.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of regulatory regions from sequence and chromatin modification signatures, and the integration of these two modalities with the 3C/HiC interaction network.
understanding the regulatory mechanisms that govern tissue-specific gene expression and the computational methods that can be used to predict the regulatory regions involved in these processes.

developing a framework for the prospective identification of regulatory regions from sequence, expression and interactome data, with the ultimate goal of improving our ability to predict the regulatory landscape of genes in the human genome.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

our proposed methods are complementary to existing methods for enhancer prediction, and are especially useful for identifying distal regulatory sequences that are associated with tissue-restricted gene expression.

the combination of chromatin state information, 3C/ 5C data and sequence motif information can be used to identify distal enhancers that are likely to be involved in tissue-specific expression of a target gene.
the combination of sequence, expression and interactome data can be used to identify putative regulatory sequences that are likely to be functionally active.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the integration of sequence, epigenome and interactome data can improve the fidelity of regulatory region prediction and the identification of tissue-specific regulatory elements.
it provides a framework for integrating sequence, chromatin modification and promoter-enhancer interactions in a unified framework.

we propose a framework to identify tissue-restricted, enhancer-like elements by integrating the following three complementary genomic modalities: (i) chromatin signatures of regulatory elements (ii) sequence conservation (iii) promoter-enhancer cross talk.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the integration of chromatin modification data, promoter-enhancer cross talk data and expression data into a single framework can improve the fidelity of prospective enhancer predictions.
the integration of multiple data modalities, in addition to sequence information, is essential in the quest for distal gene regulation.
chromatin state signatures and 5C data are complementary modalities that can be used to identify regulatory regions that co-operate in the transcriptional regulation of genes.
